subject: Path A Instability Systematic Variation of Y Variable Mediation

messages.author: d655cfdb22e0dca8
messages.subject: Path A Instability Systematic Variation of Y Variable Mediation
parts:
Hi all,

I have an interesting statistical issue that I am having some difficulties interpreting. Any guidance would be greatly appreciated !!!

I will briefly clarify that X here refers to an exposure, M to a mediator, and Y to an outcome variable. All analyses have been run with lavaan.

My team and I are running many different models where we systematically vary X, M, and Y in a classical mediation.

We are observing that for some X and M pairs, when Y is made to systematically vary but X and M remain constant, Path A coefficients change in magnitude, and statistical significance is lost. 

Other Path A terms appear robust when X and M is constant but the Y variable changes.

Furthermore, when M and Y is held constant but X systematically varies, Path B is also at times unstable (ie in coefficient magnitude and statistical significance)

This would ordinarily be unexpected under the assumption that each path estimate should reflect a unique, modular component of the model, but I understand that all Paths are estimated at once in SEM. Even still, this is tricky to interpret. My gut feeling is that I should be narrowing my focus onto Paths which are robust to slight model changes, as they represent effects which are not sensitive to subtle changes in the overall model structure or implied variance-covariance.

This would appear to me to be coherent with some arguments in the literature that effects that only exist under narrow model specifications should be treated as less robust - e.g. for Multiverse Analyses  (Steegen et al., 2016), in which robust results are those which are found consistently across data preprocessing methods; Specification curve analysis argues that models should be robust to changes in model specification; extreme bounds analyses argues that robust paths are those which are consistent while testing for all possible combinations of covariates... but these are not necessarily SEM specific.

Alternatively, one could make the claim that changing certain variables necessarily changes context - that Paths may only appear given certain measurement contexts, and instability does not necessarily imply a lack of robustness - rather, conditionality.

I cannot find any literature on this phenomenon for SEM specifically or how to interpret this and what to do more generally - other than this paper, in which authors trimmed Paths which did not drastically estimation of others, as that would point to an 'unnecessary complication' in the model. (https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-021-11364-w).  Thus, paths unstable across model configurations in my study would, according to their rationale, imply a necessary complication, in which I would maybe err on the side of not interpreting the unstable paths.

From the paper:

We initially included all paths in the model, and conducted a model trimming process: where multiple explanatory variables led to the same endogenous variable (e.g. intervention facilities and collective cleaning both lead to latrine cleanliness), we removed a path where its removal did not alter path coefficients for other explanatory variables and was therefore considered an unnecessary complication.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Path A Instability Systematic Variation of Y Variable Mediation
parts:
Structural equation models are systems of equations where model parameters link variables. Language, by contrast, is imprecise and approximate--it leaves gaps that must be filled by the receiver's beliefs, biases and past experience. Describing a system of equations using only language, and not equations, is fraught.
     You write about varying the values of your variables, and observing changes in model parameters. There are many possible reasons, depending on the exact structure of your model. Are you estimating a mean structure for this model, or just the covariance structure? Are you explicitly including error variances in your models, or relying on defaults? Is your structural model saturated, or are you modeling "full mediation," with paths from X to M and from M to Y, but with no direct path from X to Y? Some of your models may be misspecified, depending on choices you have made, and misspecification could induce bias on parameter estimates.
     If you are manipulating values of observed variables and not parameters, then the literature on the impact of unmodeled random  error may be (or may not be) relevant. Your manipulations of X, M and Y may be implicitly inducing changes in random error, which will affect *standardized* parameter estimates but will only affect *unstandardized* parameter estimates sometimes. In particular, random error in the dependent variable, Y, will not affect *unstandardized* regression parameter estimates.
     It may also be that manipu;lations of multiple variables at the same time may create offsetting effects on parameter estimates in some cases. Most variables in a structural equation model are subject to the effects of multiple model parameters, so there is not a struct 1 to 1 between values of variables and values of individual parameters, when the values of *other* parameters are left uncontrolled. Unless the model is completely specified at the level of the parameters, changing the values of the variables can have unpredictable effects.
     Rigdon, E. E. (1994). Demonstrating the effects of unmodeled random measurement error. Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 1(4), 375-380.

messages.author: d655cfdb22e0dca8
messages.subject: Re: Path A Instability Systematic Variation of Y Variable Mediation
parts:
Hi Edward,

Thank you again for your in-depth response. Lots to think about, and I really appreciate your help!!

To clarify:

  • We are estimating mean structure, and all variables are observed. Based on tutorials and discussions I’ve seen, I had understood that including a mean structure shouldn't substantially affect path estimates here, and we were interested in simple slopes and intercepts given moderated mediation - hence the estimation.

  • We’re relying on default error variances in lavaan. Our models include direct and indirect paths (X → M, M → Y, X → Y, and the mediated effect via M).

  • There doesn’t appear to be a consistent relationship between the observed instability in path coefficients and global model fit (e.g., RMSEA). Fit remains generally acceptable even in models where certain paths vary in magnitude or significance.

  • We’re using multiple imputation with the Amelia package and estimating with lavaan.mi. I also ran the same model on the same imputed dataset with and without meanstructure = TRUE this morning, which produced only minor differences in standardized estimates and errors. That said, p-values did fluctuate, which could reflect some combination of estimation uncertainty, numerical instability, or imputation-related variability...

Your point about standardized estimates being more sensitive to residual variance (and potentially error structures that shift across models) is helpful. I’ll continue exploring this by inspecting unstandardized coefficients more closely.

Based on the above, it would be hugely helpful if I am missing something that you have noticed which would be contributing to our issues!

Warm regards,
Toby
